questions.q: What does a fact table hold?
options: Measurable events — mostly foreign keys plus a handful of numeric measures like sales amount or quantity
Only text descriptions with no numeric data
A list of every user who has access to the database
The database's own configuration settings
questions.explain: Fact tables record what happened, with numbers attached, and keys pointing to the dimensions that give it context.

questions.q: What does a dimension table hold?
options: Descriptive context — attributes like product name, color, or customer details that you'd filter or group by
Only numeric measures meant to be summed
A record of every query ever run against the warehouse
Backup copies of fact table rows
questions.explain: Dimension tables answer who/what/when/where, giving meaning to the fact table's raw numbers.

questions.q: Why is a fact table typically narrow but very tall?
options: Every extra column multiplies across potentially millions of rows, so only keys and measures are kept
Fact tables are limited by SQL Server to exactly 5 columns
Fact tables never have more than 100 rows
Narrow tables are required by the CHECK constraint rules from Chapter 11
questions.explain: Keeping fact tables narrow controls storage and query cost at the scale they typically operate at.

questions.q: Why can a dimension table afford to be wide?
options: It has relatively few rows, so the extra descriptive columns are cheap to store
Dimension tables are always stored in a separate, faster database
Wide tables are required for every UNIQUE constraint to work
Dimension tables cannot have a primary key
questions.explain: Fewer rows means the cost of extra descriptive attributes stays low, unlike in a fact table.

questions.q: In AdventureWorksDW2014, what roles do FactInternetSales and DimProduct play?
options: FactInternetSales is the fact table (events and measures); DimProduct is the dimension table (descriptive product attributes)
Both are dimension tables with no fact table in the database
FactInternetSales is a dimension table; DimProduct is the fact table
They are both OLTP tables unrelated to dimensional modeling
questions.explain: This is the textbook fact/dimension pairing this lesson uses as its real example.
